q-152013.name: Question 1
q-152013.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{16}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{16} & ∼N(16\cdot 0.5,\,16\cdot {0.3}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(16\cdot 0.5,\,16\cdot 0.09) \\  & =N(8,1.44).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(8\le Y\le 9).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(8\le Y\le 9) & =P(\frac{8-8}{\sqrt{1.44}}\le Z\le \frac{9-8}{\sqrt{1.44}}) \\  & =P(\frac{0}{1.2}\le Z\le \frac{1}{1.2}) \\  & =P(0\le Z\le 0.83) \\  & =Φ(0.83)-Φ(0) \\  & =Φ(0.83)-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
Φ(0.83)=0.7967
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(8\le Y\le 9) & =Φ(0.83)-0.5 \\  & =0.7967-0.5 \\  & =0.2967.\end{aligned}
$$

then

Y=X1+X2+⋯+Xn∼N(nμ,nσ2).

Therefore, since X1,X2,…,X16 are independent and identically distributed, we have

Y=X1+X2+⋯+X16∼N(16⋅0.5,16⋅0.32)∼N(16⋅0.5,16⋅0.09)=N(8,1.44).

q-143339.name: Question 2
q-143339.worked_solution:
Recall that if ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{n}$ are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where 

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(\mu ,{\sigma }^{2}),\,1\le i\le n,
$$

then 

$$
Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{n}∼N(n\mu ,\,n{\sigma }^{2}).
$$

Therefore, since ${X}_{1},{X}_{2},…,{X}_{15}$ are independent and identically distributed, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Y={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{15} & ∼N(15\cdot 0,\,15\cdot {(\frac{2}{5})}^{2}) \\  & ∼N(15\cdot 0,\,15\cdot \frac{4}{25}) \\  & =N(0,\frac{12}{5}).\end{aligned}
$$

We wish to compute the probability $P(Y\ge 1).$ We first convert $Y$ into a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(Y\ge 1) & =P(Z\ge \frac{1-0}{\sqrt{\frac{12}{5}}}) \\  & =P(Z\ge \sqrt{\frac{5}{12}}) \\  & =P(Z\ge 0.65) \\  & =1-P(Z\le 0.65) \\  & =1-Φ(0.65)\end{aligned}
$$

From the $z$-table, we have

$$
Φ(0.65)=0.7422.
$$

Therefore,

$$
P(Y\ge 1)=1-Φ(0.65)=0.2578.
$$

Hint: A table of values of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

Recall that if X1,X2,…,Xn are independent and identically distributed (I.I.D) normal random variables, where

Xi∼N(μ,σ2),1≤i≤n,

then

Y=X1+X2+⋯+Xn∼N(nμ,nσ2).

Therefore, since X1,X2,…,X15 are independent and identically distributed, we have

Y=X1+X2+⋯+X15∼N(15⋅0,15⋅(25)2)∼N(15⋅0,15⋅425)=N(0,125).

We wish to compute the probability P(Y≥1). We first convert Y into a standard normal random variable by z-scoring:

q-143408.name: Question 3
q-143408.problem:
The time it takes John to get to school, in minutes, is normally distributed with a mean of $20\,\text{min}$ and a standard deviation of $6\,\text{min}.$
What is the probability that the sum of the times John takes to get to school on $5$ randomly selected school days is more than $90\,\text{min}?$
You may assume that the times of each day are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $z$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.04\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.5\,$ | $\,0.6985\,$ | $\,0.7019\,$ | $\,0.7054\,$ | $\,0.7088\,$ |
| $\,0.6\,$ | $\,0.7324\,$ | $\,0.7357\,$ | $\,0.7389\,$ | $\,0.7422\,$ |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ | $\,0.7704\,$ | $\,0.7734\,$ |
q-143408.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the time it took John to get to school on the $i$th day. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(20,{6}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 5.
$$

Let the random variable $W$ denote the time John takes to get to school on $5$ randomly selected days. Then, since

$$
W={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{5},
$$

we have that $W$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[W] & =5\cdot 20 \\  & =100, \\ \text{Var}[W] & =5\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =180.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
W∼N(100,180).
$$

In order to find $P(W>90),$ we convert $W$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>90) & =P(Z>\frac{90-100}{\sqrt{180}}) \\  & ≈P(Z>-0.75) \\  & =P(Z<0.75)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.75)≈0.7734.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(W>90) & ≈0.7734.\end{aligned}
$$

q-152023.name: Question 4
q-152023.problem:
In a plumbing store, the length of a water pipe is normally distributed with a mean of $2\,\text{m}$ and a standard deviation of $0.05\,\text{m}.$ If Carl bought $25$ pipes, what is the probability that the total length of the pipes he purchased is more than $49.8\,m$ and less $50.2\,m?$ It can be assumed that the lengths of pipes are mutually independent.

*Hint: A table of values of $Φ(z)$ for different values of $z$ is given below, where $Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.*

| $z$ | $\,0.00\,$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.02\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $\,0.7\,$ | $\,0.7580\,$ | $\,0.7611\,$ | $\,0.7642\,$ | $\,0.7673\,$ |
| $\,0.8\,$ | $\,0.7881\,$ | $\,0.7910\,$ | $\,0.7939\,$ | $\,0.7967\,$ |
| $\,0.9\,$ | $\,0.8159\,$ | $\,0.8186\,$ | $\,0.8212\,$ | $\,0.8238\,$ |
q-152023.worked_solution:
Let ${X}_{i}$ denote the length in the $i$th pipe. Then, we have

$$
{X}_{i}∼N(2,{0.05}^{2}),\,1\le i\le 25.
$$

Let the random variable $L$ denote the total length of $25$ randomly selected pipes. Then, since

$$
L={X}_{1}+{X}_{2}+⋯+{X}_{25},
$$

we have that $L$ is normally distributed, where

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[L] & =25\cdot 2 \\  & =50, \\ \text{Var}[L] & =25\cdot {0.05}^{2} \\  & =0.0625.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
L∼N(50,0.0625).
$$

In order to find $P(49.8<L<50.2),$ we convert $L$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring:

$$
\begin{aligned}P(49.8<L<50.2) & =P(\frac{49.8-50}{\sqrt{0.0625}}<Z<\frac{50.2-50}{\sqrt{0.0625}}) \\  & ≈P(-0.8<Z<0.8) \\  & =1-2P(Z>0.8) \\  & =1-2[1-P(Z<0.8)] \\  & =2P(Z<0.8)-1 \\  & =2Φ(0.8)-1\end{aligned}
$$

Using the $z$-table, we see that

$$
Φ(0.8)≈0.7881.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}P(49.8<L<50.2) & ≈2Φ(0.8)-1 \\  & ≈2\cdot 0.7881-1 \\  & ≈0.5762.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

In a plumbing store, the length of a water pipe is normally distributed with a mean of 2m and a standard deviation of 0.05m. If Carl bought 25 pipes, what is the probability that the total length of the pipes he purchased is more than 49.8m and less 50.2m? It can be assumed that the lengths of pipes are mutually independent.

Hint: A table of values of Φ(z) for different values of z is given below, where Φ(z) is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution.

z0.000.010.020.03
0.7 0.7580 0.7611 0.7642 0.7673
0.8 0.7881 0.7910 0.7939 0.7967
0.9 0.8159 0.8186 0.8212 0.8238
a
0.5222

0.6372

0.5762
d

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let Xi denote the length in the ith pipe. Then, we have

Xi∼N(2,0.052),1≤i≤25.

Let the random variable L denote the total length of 25 randomly selected pipes. Then, since

L=X1+X2+⋯+X25,

we have that L is normally distributed, where

E[L]=25⋅2=50,Var[L]=25⋅0.052=0.0625.

Therefore,

L∼N(50,0.0625).

In order to find P(49.8<L<50.2), we convert L to a standard normal random variable by z-scoring: P(49.8<L<50.2)=P(49.8−500.0625<Z<50.2−500.0625)≈P(−0.8<Z<0.8)=1−2P(Z>0.8)=1−2[1−P(Z<0.8)]=2P(Z<0.8)−1=2Φ(0.8)−1

Using the z-table, we see that

Φ(0.8)≈0.7881.

Therefore,

P(49.8<L<50.2)≈2Φ(0.8)−1≈2⋅0.7881−1≈0.5762.
